directions.litai: Speak in clear natural American English, as an experienced female engineer making a persuasive live demonstration to a skeptical colleague. Warm, brisk, direct, dry humor. Respond to the objection, never sound like an announcer. Do not laugh unless the words call for it.
directions.sam: Speak in natural American English, as an experienced male software engineer who has heard too many AI sales pitches. Starts irritated and dismissive, then cross-examines each answer. Wry, concise, alert; warms only when the evidence earns it. Not theatrical.

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: Picture your next release. Agents write code overnight. By morning, every change has a written promise, independent acceptance, builds on Mac, Linux and Windows, an installed package that actually ran, and a receipt naming the exact commit all of that proved. Before anyone opens CI.

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: You review promises, not diffs. Every claim carries the evidence to challenge it. Code becomes something you can regenerate; the specification is what you defend in review. That's agentic development done properly, and Literate AI is the harness that makes it real.

turns.speaker: sam
turns.text: And there it is. The usual AI slop sales pitch. Agents overnight, promises instead of diffs. I've sat through four of these this quarter.

turns.speaker: sam
turns.text: I'm Sam. C++, Make, tests. My company is in a civil war: our CTO wants agent-first everything by Q3, and I lead the holdouts. Thursday's architecture review settles it.

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: Then let's settle it with evidence instead of volume. You bring the beliefs; I'll bring a terminal. One at a time.

turns.speaker: sam
turns.text: Start here. Agent code is slop. Nobody can review ten thousand generated lines, so nobody does.

turns.speaker: litai
turns.chapter: Belief one: nobody can review it
turns.text: Agreed. So don't start with the lines; review the promise. A Component states observable behavior: a greeting card takes a name and messages, returns a greeting, an identifier and word counts. Unicode whitespace included. No implementation in it.

turns.speaker: sam
turns.text: A requirements doc. Those rot the day after the kickoff meeting.

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: Not this one; every build is pinned to it. Flavors say how: Python and Make here, C++ and CMake next door. Change the promise and every lock pinned to it goes stale until it's rebuilt and verified. Change a Flavor and you still need a real toolchain and new tests. No magic porting.

turns.speaker: sam
turns.text: Fine. How would I even get it?

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: Clone the repository, make install, then litai doctor checks the result. Sign in to your coding CLI separately. The install panel is a walkthrough; the terminal sessions are recorded runs. Anything without a terminal is a walkthrough card.

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: Nothing changes without a plan. This is the real read-only create plan, pinned to a public parent commit.

turns.speaker: sam
turns.text: And I acknowledge it, and it writes files. Every tool writes files.

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: Every tool writes files. Few tell you exactly which ones before they do.

turns.speaker: sam
turns.chapter: Belief two: it grades its own homework
turns.text: Next. The agent writes the code and the tests, then congratulates itself. Homework graded by the student.

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: Rebuild calls your chosen coding agent, with explicit permission to run generated code in this disposable project. Edited replay; the waiting is compressed.

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: The generated code: normalize the recipient, count the words.

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: And its own tests. Useful, and exactly the homework you're worried about. So they aren't the judge.

turns.speaker: sam
turns.text: Green on the first try. Which is exactly what slop looks like.

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: Green by whose cases? These acceptance cases come from the promise, inherited and unmodified: two messages, six words, this identifier. They run separately from the agent's own tests.

turns.speaker: sam
turns.text: And if your judge were too lenient, you'd be green and smiling.

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: Yes. A lenient oracle or a wrong specification still passes; no harness catches that alone. This one puts them where your reviewers can. Skips are shown as skips, not passes.

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: And when the agent is the one that's wrong, 1.2 hands it the redacted compiler error and asks for a fresh candidate, at most twice more. Then it stops and tells you why. Not in this recording; this run didn't need it.

turns.speaker: sam
turns.text: And every edit means paying for another agent run.

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: Only for what changed. Here the source came back from the cache and the rebuild took under half a minute.

turns.speaker: sam
turns.chapter: Belief three: CI is the safety net
turns.text: Now the big one. We have CI. Forty jobs, a matrix, a dashboard. That's the safety net.

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: For most teams, CI is where they first learn the truth. Push and pray, queue for an hour, find Windows red, push a fix you never ran. The green run tested a merge commit, not the one you tagged. And the pipeline file is untested code holding production keys.

turns.speaker: sam
turns.text: Rude. Accurate, but rude.

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: So move the whole gate before CI. Here's how we ship Literate AI itself. One make release-check: lint, formatting, spec and docs checks, the full test suite, a wheel, a clean install, a real installed project, live samples, and a current test receipt. Your project declares its own gate; litai release check runs it on the exact prepared commit.

turns.speaker: sam
turns.text: That's not a checklist, it's a hostage situation. Nobody runs all that before every merge.

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: No human does. That's the superhuman part, and it's stamina, not judgment. Plan, generate, build, test, accept, package, release: every stage, every time, with a record.

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: It even caught us making this film. A test helper under the driver's reviewed code changed without a fresh review pin. Red at driver review, on a laptop, before CI ever saw it.

turns.speaker: sam
turns.text: So you push a fix and pray, like the rest of us.

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: Review, re-pin, resume. Passed gates are reused while you repair, then release evidence starts clean from gate one.

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: Then it repeats on machines you already own. That Linux box and a Windows desktop become workers through private configuration. When workers build, test and run everything, your laptop doesn't even need the toolchains. Release qualify covers what this machine can, then the workers, and uses CI only for what's left. The record names the exact commit.

turns.speaker: sam
turns.text: So CI becomes...

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: A confirmation, not a discovery. This recording qualified this Mac; the remote workers are a walkthrough.

turns.speaker: sam
turns.chapter: Belief four: it's a black box
turns.text: Fine. Even when it passes, I can't see what an agent did. It's a black box with a commit message.

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: litai render html. One file per view, no server. The authority graph shows every Component, Flavor and skill, with hash-checked previews of their sources. Health views cover locks and verification.

turns.speaker: sam
turns.text: Pretty. Somebody still has to babysit it.

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: It's rebuilt from the project's own records, and a declared page that goes stale blocks qualification, like this. Build-and-test run history isn't shipped yet; the graph and health views are.

turns.speaker: sam
turns.chapter: Belief five: adoption means a rewrite
turns.text: My real code is years of C++. Adoption means a rewrite and six months of regret.

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: TinyXML2, pinned to a public commit. The plan inspects before it touches anything: preserve the original, take a recovery point, wrap its real build and tests.

turns.speaker: sam
turns.text: Which tests? Swap CTest for an agent's opinion and Thursday's over.

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: Its own CMake build and its own CTest, on preserved source. Nothing replaced, nothing rewritten.

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: Retained: baseline evidence recorded, and the original source still governs releases. You can stop here for good. Later stages exist; none are shown complete here.

turns.speaker: sam
turns.text: And agents make the same mistake every Monday. They never learn.

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: Nothing retrains a model. A lesson becomes a reviewed change to its owner: the specification if behavior was missing, a Flavor if it's platform-specific, a skill if it's technique. litai learn proposes; your review admits.

turns.speaker: sam
turns.text: So 'learning' means a pull request.

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: Exactly. Reviewable, revertible, and it outlives the model.

turns.speaker: sam
turns.text: And your framework's rules rewrite my release some Tuesday.

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: They arrive as a plan. This recorded update compares what you inherited, what you changed and what's new upstream. Conflicts wait for you.

turns.speaker: sam
turns.text: And when the CTO's agents swarm the repo, who assigns the work?

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: Your forge. GitHub or GitLab issues and pull requests, by default. Agents open reviewed pull requests like everyone else.

turns.speaker: sam
turns.chapter: Belief seven: releases are where it breaks
turns.text: Last one. Demos stop at green. Our actual release artifact is still called final-final-really-final dot zip.

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: A local wheel, built and verified; no registry upload here. A real release is plan, prepare, check, publish: a release branch, a SemVer tag, and a check of what was actually published. Tests of one commit never qualify another.

turns.speaker: sam
turns.text: So our CTO is wrong. Agents don't get to ship on vibes.

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: And the holdouts?

turns.speaker: sam
turns.text: Also wrong. Hand-reading every generated line was never the safety net. Evidence is.

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: Argument settled. Before Thursday: install it, write one Component, render the graph, qualify on two machines. Bring the receipts.

turns.speaker: sam
turns.text: And final-final-really-final dot zip retires.

turns.speaker: litai
turns.text: It had a good run. Unlike its tests.
